terms.definition: A free, open-source operating system kernel created by Linus Torvalds in 1991, derived from Unix principles. Used widely in servers, cloud infrastructure, and embedded systems.
terms.example: Amazon Linux 2 on AWS EC2 is a Linux-based OS optimized for cloud workloads.

terms.definition: The core component of Linux that acts as the bridge between applications and hardware. It manages CPU, memory, I/O devices, and system calls.
terms.example: When you run a command like ls, the shell passes the request to the kernel, which interacts with the storage hardware to list files.

terms.definition: A command-line interpreter that acts as the interface between the user and the kernel. It takes user input (commands) and passes them to the kernel for execution.
terms.example: Opening a terminal on Linux and typing pwd uses the shell to interpret and pass the command to the kernel.

terms.definition: Bourne Again SHell — the default and most widely used shell in Linux. It interprets commands and shell scripts.
terms.example: When you SSH into an EC2 instance and type commands, you are using Bash as the interpreter.

terms.definition: The hierarchical structure Linux uses to organize all files and directories, starting from the root directory (/). Everything in Linux is treated as a file.
terms.example: The path /home/ec2-user/ is inside the Linux file system, where ec2-user's home directory lives.

terms.definition: GNU's Not Unix — a collection of free software tools and utilities (like ls, cp, grep) that, combined with the Linux kernel, form a complete operating system.
terms.example: Linux = Linux Kernel + GNU utilities. Commands like ls and cat come from the GNU project.

terms.definition: Software whose source code is publicly available, allowing anyone to view, modify, and distribute it. Linux is licensed under the GPL (General Public License).
terms.example: Unlike Windows (proprietary), Linux source code can be downloaded, modified, and redistributed by anyone.

terms.definition: A complete operating system package that combines the Linux kernel with GNU tools, a package manager, desktop environment (optional), and pre-configured software.
terms.example: Ubuntu, CentOS, Amazon Linux 2, and Red Hat are all popular Linux distributions.

terms.definition: A cryptographic network protocol used to securely connect to remote Linux servers over an unsecured network. Uses port 22 by default.
terms.example: To connect to a Linux EC2 instance: ssh -i my-key.pem ec2-user@<public-ip>

terms.definition: An AWS feature that provides a browser-based SSH connection to Linux EC2 instances directly from the AWS Management Console, without requiring a separate SSH client or key pair.
terms.example: If you launched an EC2 instance without a key pair, use EC2 Instance Connect in the console to get a terminal session.

terms.definition: A set of cryptographic keys (public + private) used to authenticate SSH connections to EC2 instances. AWS stores the public key on the instance; you keep the private key.
terms.example: When launching an EC2 instance, you select or create a key pair. You use the .pem file (private key) to SSH in.

terms.definition: The default login username for Amazon Linux-based EC2 instances. Used when establishing SSH or EC2 Instance Connect sessions.
terms.example: ssh -i key.pem ec2-user@54.12.34.56

terms.definition: A protocol used to remotely connect to Windows-based systems with a graphical interface. Uses port 3389. Not applicable to Linux EC2 instances.
terms.example: To connect to a Windows EC2 instance, you use an RDP client and the instance's public IP on port 3389.

terms.definition: Print Working Directory — a Linux command that displays the full path of the current directory you are in.
terms.example: Running pwd inside /home/ec2-user/projects/ outputs: /home/ec2-user/projects/

terms.definition: Change Directory — a Linux command used to navigate between directories.
terms.example: cd .. moves one level up. cd /home/ec2-user/ goes directly to that path.

terms.definition: A running instance of a program in Linux. The kernel manages all processes, allocating CPU time and memory to each.
terms.example: When you run python3 script.py, Linux creates a process for that script which the kernel manages.

terms.definition: A foundational multi-user, multitasking operating system developed at Bell Labs in the late 1960s. Linux was designed following Unix principles and philosophy.
terms.example: macOS is also Unix-based. Linux follows the Unix philosophy: do one thing well, use text streams.

terms.definition: A temporary, sandboxed AWS lab environment used in training courses. Resources created inside a Canvas lab session are automatically deleted when the session ends.
terms.example: If you create an EC2 instance in a Canvas lab and close the lab, that instance is gone — it does not appear in your real AWS account.

terms.definition: A tool in Linux that automates the installation, updating, and removal of software packages. Amazon Linux uses yum; Ubuntu uses apt.
terms.example: sudo yum install httpd installs the Apache web server on Amazon Linux using the yum package manager.

terms.definition: A Linux server running without a graphical user interface (GUI). All operations are performed via the command line, saving significant system resources.
terms.example: Most AWS EC2 Linux instances are headless — you connect via SSH and use the command line only.

terms.definition: A unique IP address assigned to an EC2 instance that is accessible from the internet. Used to SSH into the instance from outside AWS.
terms.example: You use the public IP in your SSH command: ssh -i key.pem ec2-user@13.234.56.78

terms.definition: AWS's own Linux distribution optimized for running on EC2. It is free, maintained by AWS, and comes with many AWS tools pre-installed.
terms.example: When launching an EC2 instance, selecting 'Amazon Linux 2023' gives you AWS's optimized Linux distro.
